title: Chokepoint register: concentration metrics and the inventory of single-supplier and single-region points
why_it_matters: SIA/BCG counted more than 50 points in the chain where one region holds over 65% of supply, but we have no consistent list of which points they are, how concentration is measured, or how old the figures are. Every concentration and risk unit needs one shared register and one method.
questions: Which concentration measures should the atlas use (top-1/top-3 firm share, single-country share, HHI) and on what population (revenue, capacity, units)?
What chokepoints do SIA/BCG (2021, 2024), CSET/ETO, the US 100-day supply chain review (2021), the EU Chips Act staff working document and Japan METI each list?
Where do these lists agree and disagree, and why (definitions, year, population)?
For each listed point, what is the latest dated evidence of firm and country concentration?
Which points are single-firm (e.g. EUV scanners) vs single-country (e.g. leading-edge logic in Taiwan) vs both?
subquestions: Which chokepoints are expected to loosen by 2030 given announced capacity?
Which chokepoints are un-evidenced beyond one publisher?
primary_sources: SIA/BCG 'Strengthening the Global Semiconductor Supply Chain in an Uncertain Era' (April 2021)
SIA/BCG 'Emerging Resilience in the Semiconductor Supply Chain' (May 2024)
The White House 'Building Resilient Supply Chains, Revitalizing American Manufacturing' 100-day review (June 2021), semiconductor chapter
European Commission SWD(2022)147 accompanying the Chips Act proposal
CSET 'The Semiconductor Supply Chain: Assessing National Competitiveness' (2021) and ETO Supply Chain Explorer
OECD 'Vulnerabilities in the semiconductor supply chain' (2023) (to verify title)
Japan METI Semiconductor and Digital Industry Strategy (2021, revised 2023)
open_questions: prereq (parallel): RU-0047 value-added shares; the register should reuse its geography definitions.
Output: one table per chokepoint with metric, period, population and claim ids.

title: Critical minerals and raw materials for chips: gallium, germanium, rare earths, tungsten, antimony, helium, high-purity quartz and fluorspar
why_it_matters: Chips need small amounts of minerals whose production is concentrated (China made about 90% of gallium in 2022) and China has put several under export licensing since 2023. A shortage of a few tonnes can stop fabs or compound-semiconductor lines.
questions: Which minerals and raw materials do semiconductor fabs and packaging depend on, and in which processes (GaAs/GaN wafers, Ge substrates, W contacts and targets, rare-earth polishing and magnets, He cooling, HPQ crucibles, HF from fluorspar)?
What are the production and refining shares by country for each (USGS, EU CRM study)?
Which are under export controls (China 2023 Ga/Ge, 2024 antimony and superhard materials, 2025 rare earths and Notice 61) and what did prices and flows do afterwards?
Who produces high-purity quartz for crucibles (Spruce Pine, North Carolina; Sibelco; The Quartz Corp) and what happened after Hurricane Helene (2024)?
What share of each mineral's demand is semiconductors vs other uses?
What substitution, recycling and stockpiling options exist (US NDS stockpile, Japan JOGMEC, EU CRMA strategic projects)?
subquestions: How much gallium and germanium did China export after licensing began, month by month?
primary_sources: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries (gallium, germanium, rare earths, tungsten, antimony, helium, fluorspar, quartz)
MOFCOM/GAC announcements 2023 No. 23, 2024 No. 46, 2025 No. 61 (texts)
European Commission Critical Raw Materials Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252) and 2023 CRM study
China General Administration of Customs export statistics (HS 8112.92 gallium/germanium) (to verify code)
US DOE Critical Materials Assessment (2023)
IEA Global Critical Minerals Outlook
open_questions: Neon and specialty gases are covered in the gases/wet chemicals unit; polysilicon in the wafers unit.

title: Equipment sub-tier supply base: optics, lasers, RF power, vacuum, valves, ceramics, precision parts and subsystems
why_it_matters: Equipment makers assemble tools from subsystems made by a second tier of suppliers (RF generators, vacuum pumps, mass-flow controllers, ceramic parts, optics). Some of these are single or dual sourced, so a bottleneck two tiers down can halt tool shipments, as seen in 2021-2022.
questions: What are the main subsystem categories inside front-end tools and who supplies each (MKS Instruments, Advanced Energy, Edwards/Atlas Copco, Ebara, Horiba, Ichor, UCT, Kyocera, NGK, CoorsTek, Ferrotec, Zeiss, Trumpf, Coherent)?
Which categories are single- or dual-sourced, and how concentrated by country (Japan, US, Germany, Korea)?
How dependent are OEMs on outsourced subsystem makers (Ichor, UCT) vs in-house?
What shortages occurred in 2021-2023 (e.g. power semiconductors in tools, ceramics, valves) and how long were lead times?
How far has China localised sub-tier parts for its domestic toolmakers?
subquestions: Which sub-tier parts are named in export-control rules (e.g. components 'specially designed' for controlled tools)?
primary_sources: MKS Instruments, Advanced Energy, Ichor, Ultra Clean Holdings Form 10-K (customer concentration disclosures)
Applied Materials / Lam Research 10-K risk factors on sole-source suppliers
Atlas Copco (Vacuum Technique), Ebara, Horiba, Kyocera, Ferrotec annual reports
BIS EAR rules defining controlled components and parts for SME (Oct 2022, Oct 2023, Dec 2024)
open_questions: prereq: none new; depends on RU-0042 for tool-category map.

title: Leading-edge logic concentration: Taiwan's share, hazard exposure (earthquake, water, power) and new leading-edge capacity outside Taiwan
why_it_matters: About 92% of sub-10nm logic capacity was in Taiwan around 2019-2020. Any disruption there, from earthquakes and drought to power outages or conflict, would affect almost every advanced chip. Whether new fabs in Arizona, Japan and elsewhere change that by 2030 is the key question.
questions: What share of leading-edge logic capacity (7nm and below, 3nm and below) is in Taiwan, Korea, the US, Japan and elsewhere, now and projected to 2030?
Which leading-edge fabs outside Taiwan are operating, under construction or delayed (TSMC Arizona, Samsung Taylor, Intel Arizona/Ohio, Rapidus Hokkaido, TSMC Kumamoto/JASM, ESMC Dresden)?
What natural-hazard events have hit Taiwanese fabs (1999 Chi-Chi, 2021 drought, 2022 blackout, April 2024 Hualien quake) and what was the output impact?
How exposed are Taiwan fabs to water and power supply limits (Taiwan Water Resources Agency, Taipower data)?
What would a disruption cost (published scenario estimates) and what are their assumptions?
subquestions: How much leading-edge back-end (CoWoS) capacity sits in Taiwan vs elsewhere?
primary_sources: TSMC annual report and ESG report (fab locations, water and power use)
TSMC Arizona / JASM / ESMC announcements and CHIPS award documents
Taiwan Water Resources Agency reservoir data; Taipower outage reports (to verify)
Taiwan Central Weather Administration earthquake reports; TSMC material information filings on quake impacts (TWSE MOPS)
SIA/BCG 2024 'Emerging Resilience' capacity projections
US Commerce CHIPS Program Office progress reports
open_questions: prereq: Chokepoint register (new); geopolitical conflict scenarios belong to a risks unit, this unit covers concentration evidence and physical hazards.

title: Mature-node capacity concentration: China's buildout of 28nm-and-above capacity and dependence on Chinese legacy chips
why_it_matters: Most chips in cars, industrial and defence systems are made on older (mature) nodes. China is adding more mature-node capacity than any other country, and a 2024 US Commerce survey found 44% of companies could not tell whether their products contained Chinese chips. The concentration is shifting and its extent is unclear.
questions: What is the share of 28nm-and-above wafer capacity by country, now and projected to 2028-2030?
Which Chinese firms are adding mature-node capacity (SMIC, Hua Hong, Nexchip, CXMT for DRAM, SiC makers) and how much?
What did BIS's Section 705 legacy-chip survey (December 2024 report) find about use of PRC-made chips in US critical industries?
What trade measures target Chinese mature-node chips (Section 301 investigation launched Dec 2024, tariffs, EU responses)?
How dependent are automotive and industrial chip buyers on specific mature-node suppliers (e.g. the 2025 Nexperia dispute)?
subquestions: How are mature-node wafer prices responding to China's capacity additions?
primary_sources: BIS 'Legacy Chips' public report (December 2024) and press release on bis.gov
USTR Section 301 investigation on Chinese legacy chips (Federal Register, Dec 2024)
SMIC and Hua Hong annual reports (HKEX)
SEMI World Fab Forecast public releases (capacity by region and node band)
Netherlands Ministry of Economic Affairs order on Nexperia under the Goods Availability Act (30 Sept 2025) and its suspension
European Commission / European Semiconductor Board supply-chain monitoring outputs (to verify)
secondary_sources: Rhodium Group / CSIS analyses of Chinese legacy capacity
open_questions: prereq: Fab capacity structure unit (new) for node-band definitions.

title: China's localisation by value-chain stage: domestic share of equipment, materials, EDA, IP, foundry and packaging
why_it_matters: China buys about a third or more of the world's chip equipment and is trying to replace foreign suppliers at every stage. How far it has got, stage by stage, determines both how effective export controls are and how the global supplier base will look in ten years.
questions: What share of China's equipment purchases come from domestic toolmakers, by tool category (etch, deposition, clean, CMP, lithography, metrology, test)?
What share of China's materials use (wafers, resists, gases, targets, CMP) is domestically supplied?
What is the domestic share of EDA and IP use in China?
Which Chinese firms lead each stage and what capability gaps remain (e.g. lithography, advanced metrology)?
How are localisation targets set and funded (Big Fund I-III, local government funds, procurement guidance)?
subquestions: How reliable are the localisation-rate figures published by Chinese brokers and associations?
primary_sources: Annual reports of Naura, AMEC, Piotech, ACM Research (Shanghai), Hwatsing, Empyrean (SSE/SZSE)
China Semiconductor Industry Association (CSIA) annual reports (to verify public availability)
China Customs import data for HS 8486 (semiconductor manufacturing equipment)
SEMI WWSEMS China billings
US-China Economic and Security Review Commission reports and hearings
secondary_sources: CSET translations of Chinese policy documents
open_questions: prereq: EDA software market (RU-0006) and Semiconductor IP unit (new).
Contradictions between Chinese broker and Western estimates should be recorded, not resolved by judgment.

title: Supplier qualification and switching costs: why concentration persists (copy-exactly, PCNs, automotive requalification)
why_it_matters: Concentration persists partly because changing a supplier of a chemical, tool, fab or package takes months to years of qualification. The size of that lock-in explains why second sources are rare and why disruptions last so long.
questions: How long does it take to qualify a new material, gas or chemical supplier at a fab, and what steps are involved?
What does moving a chip to a second foundry or OSAT involve (re-design, re-qualification, cost, time)?
What do product change notification (PCN) rules require (JEDEC J-STD-046, AEC-Q100/Q101 requalification triggers)?
How does 'copy exactly' and similar practices restrict tool and material changes?
What dual-sourcing practices did buyers adopt after 2021 and how common are they?
subquestions: Which industries (automotive, medical, aerospace/defence) have the longest requalification cycles and why?
primary_sources: JEDEC J-STD-046 (customer notification of product/process changes)
Automotive Electronics Council AEC-Q100 / AEC-Q006 documents
SEMI standards on supplier change notification (to verify, e.g. SEMI E-series or C-series)
Company 10-K risk factors on single-source qualification (Intel, TI, NXP, Entegris)
secondary_sources: SemiEngineering and EE Times coverage of requalification
open_questions: INT-0019 asks the same question of practitioners; answers go there if not public.
prereq: Chokepoint register (new)

title: IC substrates and packaging materials: ABF and BT substrates, glass cores, leadframes, bonding wire, mold compounds and build-up film
why_it_matters: Advanced chips need package substrates built with Ajinomoto build-up film (ABF), made by a handful of firms in Japan, Taiwan and Korea. Substrates were a shortage item in 2021-2022 and constrain AI packaging, and glass substrates may reshuffle the supplier base.
questions: Who makes ABF and BT substrates (Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB, Kinsus, AT&S, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, LG Innotek, Simmtech) and what are their shares and plant locations?
Who supplies the key inputs (Ajinomoto ABF film, Mitsubishi Gas Chemical BT resin, glass cloth such as Nittobo T-glass) and how concentrated are they?
How large is the substrate market and how did lead times and prices move in 2021-2025?
What is the status of glass-core substrates (Intel, SKC Absolics, Samsung) and panel-level substrates?
Who supplies leadframes, bonding wire, mold compounds, underfill and solder (Mitsui High-tec, Heraeus, Tanaka, Resonac, Sumitomo Bakelite) and how concentrated is each?
Is there any substrate capacity in the US/Europe/India and what subsidies support it?
subquestions: Is the 69% Japan/Korea/Taiwan substrate share (CLM-0540) still current?
primary_sources: Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB, Kinsus, AT&S annual reports
Ajinomoto annual report / IR (ABF business)
Nittobo annual report (glass fabric)
IPC 'North American Advanced Packaging Ecosystem Gap Assessment' (2021)
US CHIPS award to Absolics (Covington, Georgia) and NAPMP substrate programme
SEMI packaging materials releases (with TECHCET)
secondary_sources: TPCA Taiwan PCB association statistics (to verify)
open_questions: prereq: Advanced packaging technology (RU-0036).

title: Disruption case studies 2011-2025: how chokepoints behaved in real shocks
why_it_matters: Real disruptions show which concentrations actually bite and how long recovery takes. A consistent set of case studies turns abstract concentration figures into evidence of impact.
questions: For each event, what was disrupted, for how long, and what did it do to output, lead times and prices: 2011 Tohoku earthquake (Renesas Naka, wafers, resins); 2011 Thailand floods (HDD, back-end); 2019 Japan export restrictions on fluorinated polyimide, photoresist and HF to Korea; 2020-2022 chip shortage; 2021 Texas freeze; 2021 Renesas Naka fire; 2021 Malaysia COVID lockdowns; 2022 Ukraine neon; 2023-2025 China mineral controls; 2024 Hurricane Helene (Spruce Pine quartz); 2025 Nexperia governance dispute and export halt
Which responses shortened recovery (stockpiles, second sources, localisation such as Korea's post-2019 materials programme)?
What do the cases say about which chokepoints matter most?
subquestions: How much did Korea's domestic HF and photoresist supply rise after 2019?
primary_sources: Renesas press releases and annual reports (2011, 2021)
Japan METI July 2019 announcement on export control review for Korea (three items)
Korea MOTIE materials-parts-equipment competitiveness programme reports (to verify)
USITC report on neon supply (2022-2023) (to verify title)
US Commerce RFI results on chip supply chain (Jan 2022)
Netherlands Ministry of Economic Affairs Nexperia order (30 Sept 2025)
SEMI/SIA statements on each event
open_questions: prereq: Chokepoint register; Critical minerals unit; Specialty gases unit.
Overlap risk with a risks-dimension unit: this unit records the evidence, risks units assess forward likelihood.

title: Chokepoint scorecard synthesis: consistent concentration metrics per stage, dated and sourced
why_it_matters: After the stage and segment units are done, the atlas needs one consistent table of concentration at every stage, computed by code from verified claims, so readers can compare chokepoints on the same basis.
questions: For each value-chain stage and segment, what are top-1, top-3 and single-country shares and HHI on a stated population and year?
Which points have changed most since 2019 and in which direction?
Which chokepoints remain unevidenced or rely on a single publisher?
Where do chokepoints coincide with export-control coverage?
subquestions: Which figures need interview confirmation?
primary_sources: Verified claims from the chokepoint register and all segment units (no new external source expected)
CSET/ETO Supply Chain Explorer for cross-check
open_questions: prereq: Chokepoint register; all segment units in value_chain and supply_chain_concentration.
Arithmetic must be done in irs code, not by the researcher.

title: Pre-competitive research stage: consortia, national labs and university programmes and how they feed industry
why_it_matters: New processes, tools and materials are first proven in shared research centres such as imec, ITRI and CEA-Leti before companies adopt them. Who funds these centres and who gets access shapes which countries and firms reach new technology first.
questions: What are the major pre-competitive research organisations (imec, CEA-Leti, Fraunhofer, ITRI/TSRI, AIST/LSTC, Albany NanoTech, NSTC/Natcast, SRC, KAIST/KETI, IME Singapore, China ICRD/Zhangjiang Lab) and their budgets?
How are they funded (government, member fees, contract R&D) and who are their members?
What role did SEMATECH, JESSI and VLSI Project play historically?
How does technology move from consortia into production (pilot lines, licensing, staff transfer)?
What are the EU Chips Act pilot lines and the US NSTC/NAPMP facilities, and what have they received?
subquestions: Are Chinese firms members of imec or other Western consortia, and have controls changed that?
primary_sources: imec, CEA-Leti, Fraunhofer, ITRI annual reports
Natcast / NSTC strategic plan and NIST CHIPS R&D documents
European Commission Chips JU pilot line announcements
Japan LSTC / Rapidus METI subsidy documents
SRC annual report
IEEE IRDS roadmap
open_questions: Overlaps RU-0014/RU-0020 on public money; this unit maps roles, not totals.

title: Chip design stage map: who designs chips, where design happens, and what a design costs
why_it_matters: Design is about half of the industry's value added, but we have little evidence on where design engineers sit (US, Taiwan, China, Israel, India, Europe), how design work is split between companies and design-service houses, and what a design costs at each node.
questions: How many chip-design companies are there by country and how is fabless revenue distributed (US, Taiwan, China, Europe, Israel, Japan, Korea)?
Where are design centres located, especially multinational design centres in India and Israel, and how many engineers work there?
What does a chip design cost by node (published estimates, and their methods), and what share is software, IP, verification and masks?
What steps make up the design flow and which are outsourced to design-service houses?
How many tape-outs happen per year by node (foundry disclosures, ESD, analyst estimates)?
Which directories enumerate design companies (GSA members, CSIA IC design branch, TSIA IC design committee, India ISM design-linked incentive recipients)?
subquestions: What share of design value is captured by system companies' in-house teams vs fabless firms?
primary_sources: TSMC annual report (customers and product counts)
China Semiconductor Industry Association IC design branch annual statistics (to verify)
Taiwan TSIA / ITRI IEK industry yearbook (to verify)
India Semiconductor Mission Design Linked Incentive (DLI) scheme approvals
Israel Innovation Authority semiconductor reports (to verify)
US BLS OEWS data for semiconductor engineers; SIA workforce reports
IBS/IBS-derived design cost figures only as estimates (label)
open_questions: Design-data handoff is RU-0034; custom silicon is RU-0045.
The 2019-era 'US$1bn per leading SoC' figure (CLM-0413) needs a current source.

title: Semiconductor IP market: processor, interface and foundation IP vendors, RISC-V and concentration
why_it_matters: Most chips reuse licensed design blocks (processor cores, interfaces, memory compilers). Arm dominates processor IP and a few firms dominate interface IP, while RISC-V is an open alternative China and others are adopting. The IP layer is a chokepoint for both cost and access.
questions: How large is the semiconductor IP market and how is it segmented (processor, interface, foundation/physical, analog/mixed-signal, security)?
What are the shares of Arm, Synopsys IP, Cadence IP, Imagination, CEVA, Alphawave, Rambus, Arteris and Chinese vendors (VeriSilicon)?
How widely is RISC-V used, by whom, and what is RISC-V International's governance and membership (Swiss move 2020)?
Which IP is foundry-provided (standard cells, memory compilers) vs third-party?
What access restrictions apply to IP licensing to Chinese customers?
subquestions: How much of Arm's royalty revenue comes from each end market?
primary_sources: Arm Holdings Form 20-F (licence vs royalty revenue, end markets)
Synopsys and Cadence 10-K (IP revenue)
CEVA, Rambus, Arteris 10-K; VeriSilicon (SSE 688521) and Andes (TWSE) annual reports
ESD Alliance EDMD (SIP category)
RISC-V International membership and annual report
open_questions: Royalty economics sit in RU-0024.

title: Mask-making stage: captive vs merchant mask shops, mask blanks, pellicles, mask writers and inspection
why_it_matters: Every chip layer needs a photomask, and a leading-edge mask set costs millions of dollars. Mask blanks, EUV pellicles, multi-beam writers and actinic inspection each have one or two suppliers. We don't yet know how much mask making is in-house vs bought from merchant shops.
questions: How large is the photomask market and what share is captive (TSMC, Intel, Samsung) vs merchant (Photronics, Toppan Photomask, DNP, Hoya, SMIC/Chinese shops)?
Who supplies EUV and DUV mask blanks (Hoya, AGC, S&S Tech) and pellicles (Mitsui Chemicals, ASML-licensed, Canatu)?
Who supplies mask writers (IMS Nanofabrication, NuFlare, JEOL), mask inspection (KLA, Lasertec) and repair (Zeiss)?
What do eBeam Initiative Mask Makers' Surveys report on mask counts, yields, write times and EUV share?
What does a leading-edge mask set cost and how long from tape-out to masks-at-fab (INT-0015)?
Where are mask shops located and are there any in the US/EU/India for mature nodes?
subquestions: What share of leading-edge masks are made in-house (INT-0020)?
primary_sources: Photronics Form 10-K
Toppan Holdings, DNP, Hoya, AGC, Lasertec annual reports
eBeam Initiative Mask Makers' Survey (published via SPIE Photomask proceedings)
SEMI photomask market releases (to verify)
Mitsui Chemicals pellicle IR materials
open_questions: INT-0015 and INT-0020 remain open for practitioners.

title: Fab capacity structure: wafer sizes, node bands, product mix, fab counts and the 200mm ecosystem
why_it_matters: Capacity is the physical base of the industry, but it is reported in different units (200mm-equivalent wafers, 300mm wafers, by node, by product). A consistent view of how many fabs exist, what they make and at what wafer size underpins every geography and concentration comparison.
questions: How is global installed wafer capacity split by wafer size (300mm, 200mm, 150mm and smaller), by node band and by product (foundry logic, memory, analog, discrete/power, opto)?
How many fabs operate by country and owner type (foundry, IDM, memory), and how many are under construction (SEMI World Fab Forecast public figures)?
How big is the 200mm ecosystem and why does it persist (analog, power, MEMS, SiC transition to 200mm)?
How do companies report capacity (TSMC 12-inch equivalent, SEMI 200mm-equivalent) and how do we convert between them?
What are typical fab utilisation rates across the cycle and where are they disclosed?
subquestions: Which fabs are scheduled to close or convert (e.g. 150mm closures)?
primary_sources: SEMI World Fab Forecast and 300mm/200mm Fab Outlook public press releases
TSMC, UMC, GlobalFoundries, SMIC annual reports (capacity in wafer-equivalents and utilisation)
Memory makers' filings (Samsung, SK hynix, Micron) on wafer capacity (to verify disclosure)
US Census Survey of Plant Capacity Utilization (NAICS 334413) (to verify series)
Japan METI Current Production Survey (semiconductor devices) (to verify)
secondary_sources: Knometa Research IC capacity reports (to verify)
open_questions: RU-0047 reconciles regional shares; this unit supplies units and definitions.

title: Test stage: wafer probe, final test, burn-in and system-level test; ATE, probe cards and independent test houses
why_it_matters: Every chip is tested at least twice, and AI chips need far longer test times; test equipment grew about 55% in 2025. Test is split between OSATs, independent test houses and chipmakers, and the tester and probe-card markets are each dominated by two or three firms.
questions: How are test insertions structured (wafer sort/probe, final test, burn-in, system-level test) and how does test time differ for AI accelerators and HBM?
What are the shares of ATE vendors (Advantest, Teradyne, Cohu) by segment (SoC, memory) and of probe-card makers (FormFactor, Technoprobe, MJC, Japan Electronic Materials)?
Who performs test: OSATs, independent test houses (KYEC, Sigurd, Ardentec), IDMs in-house, foundries (CoWoS known-good-die)?
What is the size of the test services market and where is test capacity located?
How is test data shared across companies for multi-die packages (INT-0017)?
subquestions: Is system-level test moving from OEMs to chip vendors and OSATs?
primary_sources: Advantest annual report and IR (SoC vs memory tester sales)
Teradyne and Cohu Form 10-K; FormFactor 10-K; Technoprobe (Euronext Milan) annual report
KYEC and Sigurd annual reports (TWSE)
SEMI WWSEMS test equipment segment
IEEE Heterogeneous Integration Roadmap test chapter
open_questions: Test data flows are in RU-0035.

title: Silicon wafers and polysilicon: suppliers, shares, 300mm capacity and SOI/epi wafers
why_it_matters: All chips start as a silicon wafer, and five firms make most of them, with semiconductor-grade polysilicon even more concentrated. Firm-level shares were unknown after discovery (CLM-0569).
questions: What are the revenue and area shares of Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, GlobalWafers, Siltronic, SK Siltron and Chinese makers (NSIG, Zhonghuan/TCL, Eswin)?
What are silicon wafer shipments (MSI) and revenue by year from SEMI SMG, and by size (300mm, 200mm, SOI, epi)?
Who makes semiconductor-grade polysilicon (Wacker, Hemlock, Tokuyama, Mitsubishi Materials, OCI/others) and what share each?
Who supplies SOI wafers (Soitec) and specialty wafers, and what is their share?
What long-term agreements and prepayments exist between wafer makers and fabs?
Where is wafer capacity being added (GlobalWafers Texas, Siltronic Singapore, SK Siltron US, China)?
subquestions: How much Chinese wafer capacity qualifies at leading-edge fabs?
primary_sources: SEMI Silicon Manufacturers Group (SMG) quarterly wafer shipment releases
SUMCO, GlobalWafers, Siltronic, Soitec, Shin-Etsu annual reports (contract liabilities, LTAs)
Wacker Chemie and Tokuyama annual reports (semiconductor-grade polysilicon)
US CHIPS awards to GlobalWafers and SK Siltron (to verify)
NSIG (SSE 688126) annual report
secondary_sources: Siltronic IR presentations on market shares
open_questions: Contract terms link to INT-0019.

title: Specialty gases and wet chemicals: electronic gases, neon and noble gases, fluorine chemistry, ultrapure acids and purifiers
why_it_matters: Fabs use dozens of electronic gases and ultrapure chemicals. Some (neon, fluorinated gases, high-purity HF) have few producers or purifiers in few countries, and 2019 (Japan-Korea) and 2022 (Ukraine neon) showed how quickly they become bottlenecks.
questions: Who are the main electronic-gas suppliers (Linde, Air Liquide, Air Products, Taiyo Nippon Sanso, SK Specialty, Resonac, Kanto Denka, Merck) and their shares?
Where are neon, krypton and xenon produced and purified, and how did shares shift after 2022 (resolving CON-0011: USITC ~50% vs TrendForce ~70%)?
Who supplies ultrapure wet chemicals (HF, sulfuric, hydrogen peroxide, ammonia, IPA) and where (Stella Chemifa, Morita, BASF, Kanto Chemical, Soulbrain, Dongwoo Fine-Chem)?
How do on-site gas plants and bulk supply contracts work at fabs?
Which gases face regulatory pressure (EU F-gas Regulation 2024/573, PFAS restriction) and what substitutes exist?
subquestions: How much did Korean HF localisation after 2019 change supply shares?
primary_sources: Linde, Air Liquide, Air Products, Nippon Sanso Holdings annual reports (electronics segment)
Stella Chemifa, Morita, Kanto Denka, Soulbrain annual reports
USITC documents on neon supply (2022) (to verify)
EU F-gas Regulation (EU) 2024/573 text and ECHA PFAS restriction proposal
Japan METI 2019 export control notice on hydrogen fluoride, fluorinated polyimide and resists
secondary_sources: TECHCET gases and wet chemicals releases
open_questions: Environmental compliance depth sits in RU-0032.

title: Lithography materials: photoresists (KrF, ArF, EUV incl. metal-oxide), ancillaries and developers
why_it_matters: Photoresists are made almost entirely by Japanese firms and EUV resists are a new battleground (chemically amplified vs metal-oxide). Japan used resist export licensing against Korea in 2019, which proved the chokepoint.
questions: What are the shares of JSR, TOK, Shin-Etsu, Sumitomo Chemical, Fujifilm, DuPont, Merck and Dongjin in each resist type (g/i-line, KrF, ArF dry/immersion, EUV)?
Who is developing EUV metal-oxide resists (Inpria/JSR, Lam dry resist) and what adoption is disclosed?
How large is the photoresist and ancillaries market (SEMI/TECHCET categories)?
What was the effect of JSR's 2024 take-private by JIC on the industry?
How far have China's resist makers progressed (Beijing Kehua, Nata Opto, Xuzhou B&C)?
subquestions: Where are resist factories located outside Japan?
primary_sources: TOK, Shin-Etsu, Sumitomo Chemical, Fujifilm annual reports
JSR tender-offer documents and JIC press releases (2023-2024)
Lam Research disclosures on dry resist
Japan METI 2019 notice on resists to Korea

title: Other fab consumables: CMP slurries and pads, sputtering targets, deposition precursors, quartz and ceramic parts
why_it_matters: Beyond wafers, gases and resists, fabs depend on polishing slurries and pads, metal targets, precursors for thin films, and quartz and silicon carbide parts. Several have two or three suppliers and some depend on critical minerals.
questions: Who supplies CMP slurries and pads (CMC/Entegris, Fujimi, Resonac, DuPont, Fujibo) and with what shares?
Who supplies sputtering targets (JX Advanced Metals, Honeywell, Tosoh, Konfoong, Linde) and which metals (Ta, W, Co, Cu, Ru)?
Who supplies ALD/CVD precursors (Merck/Versum, Air Liquide, Adeka, SK Trichem, DNF, Entegris)?
Who supplies quartz ware, silicon and SiC chamber parts (Heraeus, Tosoh Quartz, Ferrotec, Hana Materials, Coorstek)?

title: System integration stage: EMS/ODM board assembly, AI server assembly and how chips reach finished products
why_it_matters: Most chips are mounted on boards by contract manufacturers (Foxconn, Pegatron, Jabil, Flex, Quanta, Wiwynn) rather than by the brands that sell the product. These firms decide sourcing for some parts, carry inventory and now assemble most AI servers, but their role in chip demand is not mapped.
questions: Who are the largest EMS and ODM providers and their revenue, and what share of electronics assembly do they perform?
How are chips procured for EMS-built products (OEM-consigned vs EMS turnkey buy, 'controlled' vs 'uncontrolled' parts)?
Who assembles AI servers and racks (Foxconn/Hon Hai, Quanta, Wiwynn, Wistron, Supermicro, Dell) and in which countries (Taiwan, Mexico, US, Malaysia, Vietnam)?
How much chip inventory do EMS firms hold and who carries the risk?
Where is EMS capacity shifting (China+1 to Vietnam, India, Mexico)?
subquestions: Is ASE's EMS arm (USI) a sign of back-end/EMS convergence?
primary_sources: Hon Hai, Quanta, Wiwynn, Pegatron annual reports (TWSE)
Jabil, Flex, Sanmina, Celestica 10-K/annual reports
India PLI scheme for electronics manufacturing (MeitY) approvals
Vietnam General Statistics Office electronics exports (to verify)
secondary_sources: New Venture Research EMS rankings (to verify)
open_questions: Chip buyers' sourcing behaviour (INT-0003) is also relevant to a participants unit.

title: Post-sale and end-of-life: product longevity, obsolescence and last-time buys, authorised aftermarket, reclaimed chips and e-waste
why_it_matters: After a chip is sold, it can live 15-30 years in cars, planes or factories, long after the maker stops producing it. Obsolescence management, the authorised aftermarket and recovered chips are where supply risk and counterfeits concentrate, and this end of the chain is not yet mapped.
questions: How do chipmakers discontinue products (end-of-life notices, last-time-buy windows, JEDEC J-STD-048) and how long are longevity programmes (NXP, ST, TI, Microchip)?
Who runs the authorised aftermarket (Rochester Electronics, Flip Electronics) and how large is it?
How are chips reharvested from scrap, and how does that feed counterfeits?
How much semiconductor content is in e-waste, and what is recovered (precious metals, gallium, rare earths)?
What do defence obsolescence programmes (DMSMS, GIDEP) show about the scale of the problem?
subquestions: Do EU e-waste (WEEE) or right-to-repair rules touch chip supply?
primary_sources: JEDEC J-STD-048 (product discontinuance)
Chipmaker product-longevity programme pages (company_documentation)
US DoD DMSMS guidebook (SD-22)
UN Global E-waste Monitor (UNITAR/ITU, 2024)
GAO reports on counterfeit and obsolete parts
open_questions: Equipment post-sale service belongs to RU-0021.

title: Specialised logistics: moving wafers, masks, hazardous gases and chemicals, and fab tools
why_it_matters: Wafers, masks, toxic gases and 150-tonne EUV tools all need specialised handling, packaging and transport. Discovery found no evidence on who provides it or how many alternatives exist (CLM-0568).
questions: Which firms provide semiconductor logistics (tool moves and installation logistics, cleanroom-compatible freight, hazardous gas cylinders/ISO containers, temperature-controlled chemicals)?
How are EUV and other large tools shipped (air freight, charters), and by whom?
Who makes wafer carriers and shippers (FOUPs, FOSBs: Entegris, Shin-Etsu Polymer, Miraial, Gudeng) and how concentrated is supply?
Which hazardous-material transport rules apply (UN Model Regulations, IATA DGR, ADR) and how do they constrain routes?
How concentrated are air-freight routes for chips (e.g. Taiwan, Malaysia, Korea hubs)?
subquestions: Which logistics chokepoints appeared in 2020-2022?
primary_sources: Entegris 10-K (wafer handling)
Gudeng Precision and Miraial annual reports
Logistics providers' semiconductor service pages (company_documentation; label as reported claims)
UN Recommendations on the Transport of Dangerous Goods (Model Regulations)
IATA cargo statistics on semiconductors (to verify)
secondary_sources: Industry press on EUV tool shipment logistics
open_questions: INT-0021 remains open for practitioners.

title: Fab construction and facility systems: EPC contractors, cleanrooms, ultrapure water, sub-fab, abatement and power
why_it_matters: A leading fab costs US$5-20bn and a large share goes to the building and its systems (cleanrooms, ultrapure water, exhaust abatement, power). A small set of specialist contractors and suppliers builds most fabs, and their capacity limits how fast new fabs open.
questions: Who designs and builds fabs (Exyte, Jacobs, Fluor, Kajima, Taisei, United Integrated Services, Samsung C&T) and in which regions?
Who supplies cleanroom systems, ultrapure water (Kurita, Organo, Veolia), abatement (Edwards, Ebara, DAS) and fab automation?
What share of fab capex goes to buildings and facilities vs tools?
How long does fab construction take by country and what causes delays (permits, labour, power)?
How much water and power does a fab use and how are utilities secured?
subquestions: Is the SEMI 'fab facilities' equipment segment comparable with EPC revenue?
primary_sources: Exyte (M+W) annual report
Kurita, Organo annual reports (electronics segment)
United Integrated Services annual report (TWSE)
SEMI World Fab Forecast construction spending releases
US CHIPS award documents (construction timelines)
TSMC ESG report (water and power)
secondary_sources: SIA reports on fab construction timelines by country (to verify)

title: HBM manufacturing and supply chain: TSV stacking, base dies, bonding methods, yields and qualification
why_it_matters: High-bandwidth memory is stacked DRAM that sits next to AI processors. Only three firms make it, qualification with GPU makers decides who sells, and the base die is moving to foundries, which changes who controls the product.
questions: What are HBM generations (HBM3, HBM3E, HBM4) and their JEDEC specs, stack heights and bandwidth?
What bonding methods do SK hynix (MR-MUF), Samsung and Micron (TC-NCF) use, and when does hybrid bonding arrive?
Who makes the HBM4 base (logic) die: memory makers in-house or foundries (TSMC)?
What are HBM supply shares, capacity (wafers per month), and qualification status with NVIDIA/AMD/custom ASICs?
Which equipment and materials are HBM-specific (TC bonders: Hanmi, Hanwha, ASMPT; underfill; TSV tools)?
Is China (CXMT) developing HBM, and what export controls apply to HBM?
subquestions: How are known-good-die tests shared between HBM maker and package integrator (INT-0017)?
primary_sources: JEDEC JESD238 (HBM3) and JESD270-4 (HBM4) public summaries
SK hynix, Samsung Electronics, Micron annual reports and earnings calls
BIS December 2024 rule on HBM export controls (Federal Register)
Hanmi Semiconductor annual report (DART)
open_questions: prereq: none new. Demand side is RU-0016.

title: Leading-edge process capability by manufacturer: 3nm/2nm-class nodes, yields, and China's non-EUV path
why_it_matters: Only a few companies can make the most advanced chips, and whether Intel, Samsung, Rapidus or SMIC can catch TSMC decides future concentration. RU-0038 covers generic technology transitions; this unit compares what each firm actually ships.
questions: Which firms have 3nm-class and 2nm-class processes in volume production, with what transistor architecture and backside power, and since when (TSMC N3/N2/A16, Samsung SF3/SF2, Intel 18A/14A, Rapidus 2HP)?
What density and performance comparisons are available from independent teardown/analysis (TechInsights) rather than marketing?
What yields or customer wins are disclosed for each node?
How far has SMIC progressed with DUV multipatterning (7nm/5nm-class) and at what cost/yield (teardowns of Huawei chips)?
What is the typical time lag between leaders and followers, historically and now?
subquestions: Is 'node' naming comparable across firms (ENT-0074)?
primary_sources: TSMC, Intel, Samsung annual reports and technology symposium materials (company_documentation)
IEEE IEDM and VLSI Symposium papers
IRDS More Moore chapter
Rapidus/METI subsidy documents
BIS rules citing SMIC 7nm (Entity List notices)
open_questions: Marketing claims must be recorded as reported_claim.

title: Chiplets and heterogeneous integration: die-to-die standards (UCIe, BoW), chiplet marketplaces and design implications
why_it_matters: Chips are increasingly built from several smaller dies ('chiplets') joined in one package. Standards such as UCIe could let dies from different vendors be mixed, which would change who can compete, but real multi-vendor use is still unclear.
questions: What die-to-die interfaces exist (UCIe, BoW, AIB, proprietary NVLink-C2C, Infinity Fabric) and who governs them?
Which products use chiplets and are any multi-vendor chiplet products shipping?
What design, test and known-good-die requirements do chiplets add?
What are China's chiplet standards and strategy (e.g. Chiplet Advanced Communication Standard) as a workaround for node limits?
Which firms supply chiplet IP and interconnect (Alphawave, Eliyan, Synopsys, Cadence)?
primary_sources: UCIe Consortium specifications and member list
OCP Open Domain-Specific Architecture (ODSA) BoW specification
AMD and Intel 10-K / product documentation
China Computer Interconnect Technology Alliance chiplet standard (to verify)

title: Wide-bandgap and compound semiconductors: SiC, GaN, GaAs and InP value chains from substrate to device
why_it_matters: Silicon carbide and gallium nitride power chips drive EVs and fast chargers; GaAs and InP drive RF and optical links. They have their own substrate makers, fabs and chokepoints (e.g. Chinese SiC substrate price cuts, Wolfspeed's 2025 restructuring, China's gallium controls).
questions: Who makes SiC substrates and epitaxy (Wolfspeed, Coherent, SICC, TankeBlue, SK Siltron, Resonac) and what are their shares?
Who makes SiC and GaN power devices (Infineon, STMicro, onsemi, Rohm, Wolfspeed, Navitas, Innoscience) and where?
How fast is SiC moving from 150mm to 200mm and how have prices changed with Chinese capacity?
Who makes GaAs and InP wafers and RF/optical devices (Sumitomo Electric, AXT, Freiberger, WIN Semi, Qorvo, Skyworks) and how does gallium supply affect them?
What happened to Wolfspeed in 2025 and what does it mean for Western SiC supply?
primary_sources: Wolfspeed 10-K and Chapter 11 filings (2025)
Infineon, STMicro, onsemi, Rohm annual reports
SICC (SSE 688234) annual report
AXT 10-K (China subsidiary and gallium)
WIN Semiconductors annual report
secondary_sources: Yole power and compound semiconductor reports
open_questions: prereq: Critical minerals unit (gallium).

title: Specialty and mature process platforms: BCD, embedded NVM, RF-SOI, FD-SOI, image sensors and MEMS
why_it_matters: Cars, phones and factories rely on specialised processes (power-management BCD, embedded flash for MCUs, RF-SOI for radios, image sensors, MEMS) that only some foundries offer. These platforms explain why mature-node capacity is not interchangeable.
questions: Which foundries and IDMs offer each specialty platform and at which nodes (TSMC, UMC, GlobalFoundries, Tower, Vanguard, Hua Hong, X-FAB, STMicro, Samsung)?
How are image sensors made (stacked CIS, Sony and Samsung) and where?
What are the MEMS foundries and IDMs (Bosch, STMicro, TDK, Silex) and how is MEMS counted in market statistics?
How hard is it to move a specialty-process chip between foundries?
Where does China have or lack specialty capacity?
primary_sources: GlobalFoundries, UMC, Tower, X-FAB, Vanguard annual reports (technology platform revenue splits)
Sony Group annual report (I&SS segment)
Bosch annual report (semiconductors)
open_questions: Israel (Tower) is covered here as a jurisdiction of specialty foundry capacity.

title: Silicon photonics and co-packaged optics: technology, suppliers and fit with the chip supply chain
why_it_matters: AI clusters are moving data by light, and co-packaged optics puts optical engines next to switch and GPU chips. This pulls photonics foundries, lasers and optical packaging into the chip supply chain, with new suppliers and bottlenecks.
questions: What are silicon photonics and co-packaged optics, and which products ship (Broadcom, NVIDIA, Intel, Marvell)?
Which foundries offer silicon photonics processes (TSMC COUPE, GlobalFoundries, Tower) and who supplies lasers (InP) and fibre attach?
How is optical packaging done and by whom?
Which standards and multi-source agreements apply (OIF, CPO MSAs)?
primary_sources: Broadcom, Marvell, Coherent, Lumentum 10-K
TSMC and GlobalFoundries photonics platform documentation
OIF implementation agreements
AIM Photonics (US Manufacturing USA institute) reports

title: Manufacturing software and fab automation suppliers: MES, APC/FDC, yield software and automated material handling
why_it_matters: Fabs are run by software and robots (MES, process control, yield analysis, overhead transport). A few vendors supply these systems and some fabs build their own, which matters both for resilience and for any new supplier.
questions: Who supplies MES (Applied SmartFactory, Critical Manufacturing, Siemens Opcenter, IBM legacy), APC/FDC (Applied, PDF Solutions, INFICON), yield software (PDF Solutions, KLA, Synopsys) and AMHS (Daifuku, Murata Machinery)?
What share of fabs use in-house vs vendor systems?
How large are these markets and how concentrated?
Do export controls cover fab software and automation, and how is China localising it?
primary_sources: PDF Solutions 10-K
Daifuku annual report (cleanroom segment)
Applied Materials 10-K (AGS software)
INFICON annual report
ASMPT/Critical Manufacturing IR (to verify)
open_questions: RU-0035 covers the data flows; this unit covers the supplier landscape.

title: Technology history: wafer-size transitions, lithography generations and packaging generations and how each reshaped the supplier base
why_it_matters: Each big technology shift (150 to 200 to 300mm wafers, the abandoned 450mm, g-line to EUV lithography, wire-bond to flip-chip to 2.5D packaging) killed some suppliers and made others dominant. Knowing this helps judge which current shifts will reorder the industry.
questions: When did each wafer-size transition happen, what did it cost, and why was 450mm abandoned (G450C)?
How did the lithography market move from Nikon/Canon to ASML (immersion, EUV), with dates and shares?
How did packaging evolve (DIP, QFP, BGA, flip-chip, WLP, fan-out, 2.5D/3D) and who led each?
What does history suggest about how fast new technologies move from lab to volume?
primary_sources: ASML annual reports (historical)
Nikon annual reports (historical)
ITRS archived roadmaps
SEMATECH / ISMI 300mm transition documents
G450C consortium materials (SUNY Poly) (to verify)
secondary_sources: Academic histories of lithography (e.g. Henderson and Clark 1990)
